topic: How long new habits take to form
text:
A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis from the University of South Australia brought together 20 studies with 2,601 adults building new health habits such as healthy eating, physical activity, drinking water and flossing. The authors concluded that new health habits usually took months rather than weeks to become automatic, and that the time needed varied widely from one person to the next. They say this challenges the popular idea that a habit forms in a few weeks.

Why this matters across roles: When a client, patient or participant says a new routine still feels like hard work after a few weeks, that is common and is not a sign of failure. The authors suggest realistic expectations may help people stay motivated through the early stages.

One practical takeaway: Let people know that effort in the early months is expected, notice whether the routine happens at a steady time and place, and ask whether they chose it themselves, as self-chosen habits and stable routines were linked with stronger habits. If progress stalls or wellbeing drops, check in with the person's GP or treating team.

Where the evidence stops:
• Only four studies directly measured how long habits took to form
• Most studies had a high risk of bias, and habit strength was mostly self-reported
• The review covered building healthy habits, not stopping unwanted ones

Key source: Singh et al., 2024: https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare12232488
